questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to study and experience a culture at place where I had never been before and Japan seemed like a good fit because of its modernity and vastly different culture to the European ones

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy. The university was great at communicating and if I ever had a question they answered in no time.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The front office at my dorm were quick to give me some info about the place which was nice. The university didn't really give anything until the actual studying began.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: International Residence Chuo (on Tama campus)

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Good cooking facilities but no meal plans offered (which is completely fine)

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The campus is VERY far away from the city center (about an hour to Shinjuku) but its definitely the place to be if you want to meet people from your uni. Japan is quite closed off as a society (if you dont speak japanese) so I think I wouldn't have gotten many friends had I not stayed on campus. There were a few rules but nothing too crazy.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: People at uni in Japan are younger compared to Denmark so be prepared that most Japanese students are 18-20 years old.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: We were provided with the syllabus in advance where we could look up the contents of each course. Then you choose which courses you want and then you have a week to try and see if that course is for you - otherwise you can choose another one. I was satisfied with the ones i originally chose, but my faculty at home wouldn't let me choose the Japanese language course so i had to choose two more courses. It all worked out fine with no problems.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was the offices of the major programmes and student counseling but i don't think anyone used those services. It was easy to find information on the syllabus.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successful, i got the ones i wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The english level is horrible. There are very few courses that are offered in english so read that syllabus carefully. Some courses have a different name as to what is actually being taught - for example i chose Philosophy (thinking that is was, you guessed it, philosophy) but it turned out to be more directed towards market economy which i thought was a little strange.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Very easy level of academics, at least the ones i took. The things being taught were quite outdated and on the level of secondary education which stunned me. I don't know if it was because of the english level being low or the courses themselves but it was definitely different from uni back home in terms of substance, teaching-style and general level. Some theories being taught in some of my courses had flat out been disproved since many of the texts used were outdated (some books were from the 70s!) but when we confronted the teachers about it they just said that the book said so.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Somewhat similar but a bit more high-school type of teaching where the classes are small and the teacher wants the students to engage in discussions. You have to show up to the lectures. I think that the style depended a lot on how many people were in your class.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Philosophy, Hellenism and Islamo-Christian Thought, Social Issues, Social Inequality in Japan, Language and Culture E, Global Lecture, Global Tutorial

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The global tutorial ones were good and the teachers there were passionate and very sweet (and they actually did research on the topics they were teaching). If you want an easy one then choose Language and Culture E (it was just about Great Britain in general). Again, look at the syllabus and see if the courses sounds good to you:)

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The trains were more expensive than i anticipated (also because the cost of getting into the city from Tama Center was about 40DKK each direction, so it quickly adds up). There were some small hidden fees with the housing but nothing too expensive. I would recommend having a good amount of money for trips, experiences and shopping!

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food is very cheap compared to danish standards (surprise) it is cheaper to eat out than cooking yourself so have fun trying a bunch of different restaurants and Japanese cuisine!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were a bunch of clubs but they were not really advertised to us, you sort of had to know who to ask. Almost all of the clubs had no english speakers so it is difficult to join if you dont speak Japanese.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: No clue. There is a bunch of sports teams so try those ones. But again, if you dont speak Japanese then it will be difficult.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go explore! Go into Tokyo and experience the crazy night life, the cool cafe culture and the energy. Go to a bunch of nature spots and travel around Japan! It is such a beautiful country with so much to offer - so dont skimp out on experiences! I also went to Hong Kong and Seoul because flights were cheap and because i wanted to see more of Asia which i am so glad i did!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was okay i think. Japan is very popular right now so i knew most of the customs before i went like bowing, receiving things with two hands and covering up tattoos (thanks to social media). The only thing i really wanted to try was a traditional onsen, but i am heavily tattooed (and that is a big no-no) so no luck there (but there are more touristy ones that allow tattoos). The train system is good and the locals are sweet to help. Plus, people can see that you are a foreginer so they don't uphold you to the same standards as they do themselves. The most difficult thing was the language barrier as not a lot of Japanese people speak english. But hand gestures and Google Translate gets you very far!

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Learn Japanese. Very few students spoke english to the point where you could have a meaningful conversation. They were all so so sweet but it is quite difficult to form a deeper friendship when you dont understand each other - at least in my opinion.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
I had to get used to people staring a little bit. In the center of Tokyo its not bad at all, but in Tama Center I don't think that the locals are that used to seeing foreign faces. I was often stopped on the street by locals trying to say things to me (which was fun, cause they were super sweet). You can generally go very far with a smile and a positive attitude. 

The thing that was most challenging, apart from the language, was the lack of modernity that i am used to in Denmark. When registering to live in Tokyo everything was on paper and very old-school. It was less tech-savvy than i thought it would be.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The attention to detail and the hospitality. Everyone was so great to try to help is there was ever a small issue. I personally liked the more traditional aspect of the culture like shrines, temples the craftsmanship.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Learn at least just a little bit Japanese before going. It will help you tremendously 
2. Go on as many cool trips as possible and try to talk to people
3. Choose the easy courses and focus on being on exchange. It really is a great experience

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Think about what you want to get out of your exchange. Do you want to engage in the culture, meet people, travel, learn, immerse in school or something else? Bring your big wallet and apply for grants and scholarships.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting a bunch of new people and getting to experience a totally different culture.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Language barrier and the lack of useful academics. I think that if the housing was closer to central Tokyo it would have been a better experience in term of experiencing things. Also, the academics were pretty useless.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Just go. It's a great adventure and the worst that can happen is that you're a little sad. But then at least you're sad in Japan.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
